findings.documented: response contains a single field 'token'
findings.actual: response contains 'access_token' not 'token'
findings.how_found: logged in via Postman and inspected the raw response body
findings.impact: frontend code written against the documented field name will fail to store the token at all

findings.documented: Tokens are valid for 24 hours
findings.actual: Response contains `expires_in: 900`, indicating a 15-minute access-token lifetime
findings.how_found: logged in via Postman and inspected the raw response body
findings.impact: a frontend built on a 24h single-login assumption will silently drop the session after 15 minutes

findings.documented: not mentioned anywhere in the reference
findings.actual: exists and is required to keep a session alive past 15 minutes
findings.how_found: found 'refresh_url' in the /auth/login response body
findings.impact: without using this, no frontend can satisfy the 30-minute session requirement

findings.documented: user object contains email and name
findings.actual: user object contains only email
findings.how_found: logged in via Postman and inspected the raw response body
findings.impact: minor — any UI relying on a display name from login response has nothing to show

findings.documented: Invalidates the current token server side
findings.actual: After logging out, the previously issued access token was still accepted by `GET /v1/listings`
findings.how_found: First called `POST /auth/logout/` then then requested `GET /v1/listings` using the same access token in Postman, received 200 OK response
findings.impact: a user who logs out on a shared/public device is not actually signed out — anyone with the old token retains full access until natural expiry (15 min)

findings.documented: not documented — the reference claims no refresh flow exists
findings.actual: calling /auth/refresh issues a new access_token and refresh_token, but the previous refresh_token remains usable afterward rather than being invalidated
findings.how_found: called /auth/refresh twice using the original refresh_token both times and received valid new tokens on the second call
findings.impact: refresh tokens are never actually revoked through normal use; a leaked or old refresh_token remains valid indefinitely, since neither refresh nor logout invalidate it

findings.documented: Append API key as a query parameter: ?api_key=...
findings.actual: query parameter auth does not work at all; the server rejects it with a 401 and an explicit error message directing the client to send the key via the X-API-Key header instead
findings.how_found: sent a request using only ?api_key= with no header and received a 401 with detail explaining the header is required
findings.impact: the documented auth method is completely non-functional; any client built strictly to the documentation cannot authenticate at all

findings.documented: Collection responses contain 'total', 'page', 'page_size' and 'results'
findings.actual: The responses contain 'limit', 'offset', 'count', 'total', 'has_more', and 'results'.
findings.how_found: Called 'GET /v1/listings' without filters through Postman.
findings.impact: The frontend must use the API's offset-based pagination contract rather than the documented page-based contract.

findings.documented: returns only active listings in your city; inactive, expired and withdrawn listings are excluded server-side and anything returned is safe to show to a user
findings.actual: returned records include 'is_live': 'false' listings, meaning inactive/non-live listings are not filtered out server-side
findings.how_found: inspected 'is_live' field across returned listing records and found false values present
findings.impact: a frontend trusting the doc's claim would display inactive listings to users as if they were live; client-side filtering on 'is_live' is required

findings.documented: page parameter, 1-indexed, controls which page of results is returned
findings.actual: page parameter has no effect; pagination is controlled by offset, not page
findings.how_found: sent requests with different page values while holding other parameters constant and observed no change in returned results
findings.impact: a client built to paginate using page per the documentation would receive the same page of results repeatedly and never reach the end of the dataset

findings.documented: limit parameter, maximum 200
findings.actual: requesting with limit > 50 returns only 50 records per page; the actual maximum is 50
findings.how_found: requested limit=200, limit=100 and response returned with 'limit': 50
findings.impact: a client assuming it can pull up to 200 records per page will under-fetch and require more requests than expected; bulk pagination must account for the real cap of 50

findings.documented: 'total' is the exact number of records matching your filters; to fetch every record, divide total by limit and request that many pages
findings.actual: 'total' under-reports the real record count (no filter - 3391 reported vs 3500 actually retrievable) — the documented method for fetching all records does not work
findings.how_found: paginated using offset past the point implied by total/limit and found has_more still true
findings.impact: a client following the documented method would compute the wrong number of pages using a parameter that does nothing, and would stop short of the real dataset; has_more is the only reliable way to know pagination is complete

findings.documented: locality parameter must be an exact match, lowercase
findings.actual: locality matching is case-insensitive — 'sector 82', 'Sector 82', and 'SecTor 82' all return identical results
findings.how_found: sent the same locality value in three different casings and compared results
findings.impact: minor — the documented lowercase restriction is stricter than actual behavior; a frontend does not need to normalize casing before sending the locality filter

findings.documented: min_price and max_price filter listings by a price range, inclusive
findings.actual: neither min_price nor max_price has any effect on results — tested both at extreme low and high values with no change in the returned listings
findings.how_found: applied min_price and max_price independently at extreme values (150 and 150000000) and compared result sets, which were identical to unfiltered results in every case
findings.impact: price-range filtering does not work server-side at all; the frontend's price filter (a hard requirement) must be implemented entirely client-side against the full retrieved dataset

findings.documented: furnishing filters listings by furnishing status: unfurnished, semi-furnished, fully-furnished
findings.actual: furnishing has no effect on results — tested all three documented values, response unchanged in every case
findings.how_found: tested each documented furnishing value independently via Postman and compared result sets, which were identical
findings.impact: furnishing filtering does not work server-side; must be implemented client-side, consistent with the same gap already found in min_price and max_price

findings.documented: sort_by=posted_at sorts listings by posting date
findings.actual: posted_at sorting is mostly correct (oldest to newest) but unreliable — a subset of records appear out of chronological sequence, regardless of the order parameter
findings.how_found: requested sort_by=posted_at via Postman and inspected posted_at values across the result set, finding most records in correct chronological order but some out of place
findings.impact: a listings screen cannot fully trust server-side date sorting; sorting by posted_at should be done client-side against the full dataset to guarantee correctness

findings.documented: order parameter controls ascending (asc, default) or descending (desc) sort direction
findings.actual: order has no effect — results are always returned in ascending order regardless of the value passed
findings.how_found: tested sort_by with both asc and desc order values via Postman and compared result sets, which were identical
findings.impact: descending sort is unavailable server-side for any field; must be implemented client-side after fetching data

findings.documented: returns up to ten comparable listings — same locality, same bedroom count, price within 15%
findings.actual: returns 404 not found
findings.how_found: requested the endpoint with a valid listing_id via Postman and received a 404
findings.impact: the 'you may also like' feature suggested for the listing detail page cannot be built using this endpoint

findings.documented: the projects endpoint states total_listings 'always agrees with what GET /v1/listings?project_id=... returns'
findings.actual: project_id has no effect as a query filter on /v1/listings — the request the projects documentation references does not actually filter results
findings.how_found: requested /v1/listings?project_id=<id> via Postman and compared results to an unfiltered request; also confirmed the same project_id resolves correctly via GET /v1/projects/{project_id}, ruling out an invalid ID as the cause
findings.impact: the documented method for verifying total_listings does not work; total_listings must instead be checked by counting listings per project_id client-side against the full pulled dataset

findings.documented: rental object fields do not include is_live
findings.actual: is_live is present on rental records, same as on listings
findings.how_found: inspected rental objects in the full pulled dataset
findings.impact: an insights or filtering feature that should exclude inactive rentals cannot rely on documentation and must check is_live directly

findings.documented: price_min and price_max are in rupees
findings.actual: neither field is in raw rupees. Most projects have both fields in crores; a separate group has price_min in lakhs and price_max in crores.
findings.how_found: compared price_min/price_max under multiple unit conversions (lakhs, crores) against average real listing prices per project_id across a sample spanning the full value range
findings.impact: any calculation using these fields (e.g. costliest_project, Q7) must apply the correct per-record conversion based on which pattern the record matches, not a single fixed factor

findings.documented: price_min and price_max are in rupees
findings.actual: 3 projects (P60090, P60179, P60273) have price_min and price_max values that don't fit any tested unit conversion (crores, lakhs, or a mix) against their own linked listings' actual prices — average listing price falls outside the range under every conversion tried
findings.how_found: converted price_min/price_max under multiple unit hypotheses and compared against the average real listing price for each project_id, isolating these 3 as inconsistent under all of them while ~400 other projects fit one of two clear patterns
findings.impact: these 3 projects' price data cannot be trusted under any unit assumption; excluded from costliest_project (Q7) calculation

findings.documented: GET, POST, and DELETE /v1/favourites — save, list, and remove favourited listings
findings.actual: all three methods return 404 not found
findings.how_found: called GET, POST, and DELETE on /v1/favourites via Postman with valid auth, all returned 404
findings.impact: the documented favourites feature does not exist at all; the frontend's required saved-listings feature (Part 1) cannot be built against this endpoint.

findings.documented: returns pre-computed aggregates for your city — total_listings, median_price, median_price_per_sqft, by_locality, by_bhk
findings.actual: returns 404 not found
findings.how_found: called /v1/analytics/summary via Postman with valid auth and received 404
findings.impact: the insights screen (Part 1, requirement 6) cannot be built from this endpoint at all; every aggregate documented here must be computed client-side from the full retrieved dataset instead
